title: April in Paris
original_issue: Clef/Verve single and the Verve LP "April in Paris" (MGV 8012; Wikipedia gives the LP as 1957, the single is not dated)
personnel: Count Basie (piano); trumpets Wendell Culley, Reunald Jones, Thad Jones, Joe Newman; trombones Henry Coker, Bill Hughes, Benny Powell; saxes Marshall Royal, Bill Graham, Frank Wess, Frank Foster, Charlie Fowlkes; Freddie Green (guitar), Eddie Jones (bass), Sonny Payne (drums); arranger Wild Bill Davis
trivia: Wild Bill Davis's chart ends with Basie calling for the final chorus "one more time" and then "one more once". Thad Jones plays his "Pop Goes the Weasel" solo and Benny Powell takes the trombone bridge.

track.title: April in Paris
track.query: Count Basie and His Orchestra April in Paris 1955
track.notes: Basie orchestra, Wild Bill Davis arrangement (3:47 on the LP); not the 1930s Vernon Duke song versions by others or later Basie remakes

notes: July 1955 at Fine Sound, New York, is per Wikipedia and a secondary source; the album page's infobox lists 26 July 1955 and 4-5 January 1956 for the album as a whole, so the exact day for this track is not confirmed. Release year is uncertain: Wikipedia dates the LP 1957, Grammy Hall of Fame lists it as a 1955 single; 1956 is used here. Verve catalogue number is from Wikipedia.

title: Cry Me a River
original_issue: Liberty 55006 (45 rpm single, 1955); LP "Julie Is Her Name", Liberty LRP-3006 (December 1955)
personnel: Julie London (vocal), Barney Kessel (guitar), Ray Leatherwood (bass)
trivia: A smoky voice with just guitar and bass behind it: London's sparse reading of Arthur Hamilton's torch song, filmed in "The Girl Can't Help It" in 1956, made it a bestseller. Her version entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2001.

track.title: Cry Me a River
track.query: Julie London Cry Me a River Julie Is Her Name 1955
track.notes: Julie London, Liberty, first track of Julie Is Her Name (2:36); not Ella Fitzgerald, Joe Cocker or later versions

notes: The album page gives 8-9 August 1955 for the sessions (Western Recorders, Hollywood); the single's exact release month is not stated. The song was written by Arthur Hamilton in 1953.

title: St. Thomas
composer: Sonny Rollins (based on a traditional Caribbean folk song)
original_issue: Prestige PRLP 7079 (LP "Saxophone Colossus", March/April 1957); also Prestige 45-108 (45 rpm "St. Thomas Parts 1 & 2", 1957)
personnel: Sonny Rollins (tenor sax), Tommy Flanagan (piano), Doug Watkins (bass), Max Roach (drums)
trivia: Rollins built this calypso-flavoured theme on a Caribbean nursery song that his mother sang to him as a child. Pianist Randy Weston had already recorded it in 1955 as "Fire Down There".

track.title: St. Thomas
track.query: Sonny Rollins St. Thomas Saxophone Colossus 1956
track.notes: Prestige matrix 919 from 22 Jun 1956, as on Saxophone Colossus (6:49); not Rollins's later live or studio remakes

notes: Date, matrix and personnel from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack). The LP was released March/April 1957 per Wikipedia, so about nine months after the session; the album is in the Grammy Hall of Fame.

title: Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue
original_issue: Columbia CL 934 (LP "Ellington at Newport", November 1956)
personnel: Duke Ellington (piano) and his orchestra, with Paul Gonsalves (tenor sax solo), Cat Anderson (trumpet), Jimmy Woode (bass), Sam Woodyard (drums)
trivia: Paul Gonsalves's 27-chorus tenor solo at the 1956 Newport festival, with Ellington shouting him on, turned a 1937 piece into the revival of Ellington's career; he was on the cover of Time soon afterwards. A tape found in 1996 showed that the LP mixed live music with a studio redo and dubbed-in applause.

track.title: Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue
track.query: Duke Ellington and His Orchestra Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue Ellington at Newport 1956
track.notes: The 1956 Columbia LP version of the Newport performance (14:56); not the 1937 original, nor the 1999 complete Newport edition (14:20)

notes: Wikipedia says the band performed at Newport on 7 July 1956; the album page gives 7-8 July for the live and studio work. Because the issued LP is a composite of live tape and studio retakes, treat the date as the festival performance. Catalogue number CL 934 and the Columbia label are from general knowledge/Wikipedia infobox label; the HoF lists the track as a 1956 single.

title: Blue Train
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 1577 (LP "Blue Train", January 1958); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1691
personnel: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Curtis Fuller (trombone), John Coltrane (tenor sax), Kenny Drew (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Philly Joe Jones (drums)
trivia: Coltrane's only session as a leader for Blue Note, recorded in one day in Hackensack. Unlike his previous label, Blue Note paid the musicians to rehearse the music beforehand.

track.title: Blue Train
track.query: John Coltrane Blue Train 1957
track.notes: Blue Note master of the title track from 15 Sep 1957 (10:43); not alternate takes or Coltrane's live versions

notes: Date and personnel from jazzdisco; Wikipedia gives release as January 1958 and the Grammy Hall of Fame inducted the album in 1999. The single catalogue number (45-1691) is from earlier research.

title: Summertime
original_issue: Verve MGV 4011-2 (2-LP set "Porgy and Bess", April 1959)
personnel: Ella Fitzgerald (vocal), Louis Armstrong (trumpet, vocal), orchestra arranged and conducted by Russell Garcia; producer Norman Granz
trivia: Fitzgerald sings the lullaby and Armstrong's gravel voice and trumpet answer it, over Russell Garcia's orchestra. The recording dates from August 1957, but the double album only appeared in April 1959, which is why this is often called the 1959 version.

track.title: Summertime
track.query: Ella Fitzgerald and Louis Armstrong Summertime Porgy and Bess 1957
track.notes: Duet from the 1959 Verve album Porgy and Bess (4:58); not Armstrong's or Fitzgerald's other Summertime recordings, nor Sidney Bechet's 1939 version

notes: GAP: recorded 1957, first released 1959 (2 yrs). Wikipedia's album page gives recording dates of 18-19 Aug and 14 Oct 1957 in Los Angeles and an April 1959 release; jazz.com dates this track 18 Aug 1957. Year is set to the recording year (1957) per the brief; the user's "1959 version" refers to the release. Album in the Grammy Hall of Fame (2001).

title: I Loves You, Porgy
composer: George Gershwin, Ira Gershwin and DuBose Heyward
original_issue: Bethlehem single (May 1959); LP "Little Girl Blue", Bethlehem (February 1959)
personnel: Nina Simone (piano, vocal), Jimmy Bond (bass), Albert "Tootie" Heath (drums)
trivia: Simone's first hit was a song from Gershwin's Porgy and Bess, recorded in a late-1957 session that her label then sat on. When Bethlehem finally released it as a single in May 1959 it reached No. 18 on the pop chart and No. 2 on the R&B chart.

track.title: I Loves You, Porgy
track.query: Nina Simone I Loves You, Porgy Little Girl Blue 1957
track.notes: Nina Simone, Bethlehem, album version (4:12) from the late 1957 Beltone session; not later live or Colpix versions

notes: GAP: recorded 1957, first released 1959 (2 yrs). Recording date is only "late 1957" (Beltone Studios, New York) so no exact day is given; album released Feb 1959, single May 1959. Personnel from Wikipedia's album page. Grammy Hall of Fame lists the single as 1958. Bethlehem catalogue numbers were not found.

title: Autumn Leaves
composer: Joseph Kosma (music), Jacques Prevert and Johnny Mercer (lyrics)
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 1595 (LP "Somethin' Else", August 1958); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1737
personnel: Cannonball Adderley (alto sax), Miles Davis (trumpet), Hank Jones (piano), Sam Jones (bass), Art Blakey (drums)
trivia: Though issued as Cannonball's date, the session is as much Miles Davis's: he sits in as a sideman, takes several of the first solos and, according to the liner notes, chose most of the material. "Autumn Leaves" stayed in his own repertoire afterwards.

track.title: Autumn Leaves
track.query: Cannonball Adderley Autumn Leaves Somethin' Else 1958
track.notes: Blue Note take 2 from 9 Mar 1958 (10:55 on the LP); not the 9:33 alternate take on later issues, nor Erroll Garner's or other Autumn Leaves

notes: Date, take and issues from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack); the album, Cannonball's only one for Blue Note, was released August 1958 (Wikipedia). Davis was under contract to Columbia, hence the sideman role.

artist: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
title: Moanin'
original_issue: Blue Note BLP 4003 (LP "Moanin'", late 1958); 45 rpm Blue Note 45-1735 ("Moanin' Parts 1 & 2")
personnel: Lee Morgan (trumpet), Benny Golson (tenor sax), Bobby Timmons (piano), Jymie Merritt (bass), Art Blakey (drums)
trivia: Pianist Bobby Timmons wrote this gospel-tinged call-and-response theme, with the horns answering the piano, and it became the Jazz Messengers' signature piece. Both the single and the album are in the Grammy Hall of Fame.

track.artist: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers
track.title: Moanin'
track.query: Art Blakey and the Jazz Messengers Moanin' 1958
track.notes: Blue Note take 4 from 30 Oct 1958 (9:35 on the LP); not alternate take 2 or the shortened 45 edit

notes: Date, take and issues from jazzdisco (Van Gelder Studio, Hackensack); Wikipedia says the album was released "late 1958" while some sources give 1959. The Grammy Hall of Fame inducted the single in 1998 and the album in 2001.

title: Fever
composer: Eddie Cooley and Otis Blackwell (as John Davenport)
original_issue: Capitol single (1958; catalogue number not found)
personnel: Peggy Lee (vocal), Joe Mondragon (bass), Shelly Manne (drums); arranged by Peggy Lee and Jack Marshall; finger snaps by Howard Roberts or Lee herself
trivia: Lee strips Little Willie John's 1956 rhythm-and-blues hit down to upright bass, a minimal drum part and finger snaps, and adds new verses. It reached No. 8 on Billboard on 25 August 1958 and became her signature song.

track.title: Fever
track.query: Peggy Lee Fever 1958
track.notes: Peggy Lee's 1958 Capitol single recording; not Little Willie John's 1956 original, Ray Charles's or Madonna's versions

notes: Date (19 May 1958) is from peggylee.com, where Lee recounts the session; a discography lists Jack Marshall conducting, Joe Mondragon on bass and Shelly Manne on drums for that date, and Wikipedia agrees on bass and drums. The finger-snap credit is split between Howard Roberts and Lee in the sources. Capitol catalogue number and exact length were not found. Duration approximate (not taken from a source).

title: Chega de Saudade
composer: Antonio Carlos Jobim and Vinicius de Moraes
original_issue: Odeon 14.360 (78 rpm single, b/w "Bim Bom", 1958); later LP "Chega de Saudade", Odeon (14 April 1959)
personnel: Joao Gilberto (vocal, guitar), with orchestral accompaniment arranged by Antonio Carlos Jobim
trivia: Often called the first bossa nova record: Gilberto's soft, off-beat guitar and almost spoken singing set the style. Elizeth Cardoso had recorded the Jobim song first, but his single was the hit that made bossa nova a genre.

track.title: Chega de Saudade
track.query: Joao Gilberto Chega de Saudade 1958
track.notes: Joao Gilberto's 1958 Odeon single version (about 2:01); not Elizeth Cardoso's earlier recording nor Getz/Gilberto remakes

notes: Wikipedia describes Gilberto's as the second recording of the song, in 1958, after Cardoso (recorded 1957, released 1958). Single catalogue number conflicts between sources (Odeon 14.360 on Wikipedia; 12725/6 in a Brazilian article) and the exact release month (July or August 1958) is uncertain. The orchestra credit is not confirmed against a session sheet. The Grammy Hall of Fame inducted the single in 2000. Diacritics omitted in the artist and title fields.

title: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes
original_issue: Mercury 71435 (45 rpm single, b/w "Come On Home", 1959); LP "What a Diff'rence a Day Makes!", Mercury (1959)
personnel: Dinah Washington (vocal), Belford Hendricks (arranger, conductor); album credits include Joe Zawinul (piano), Kenny Burrell (guitar), Milt Hinton (bass), Panama Francis (drums), Jerome Richardson (flute) and Charles Davis (baritone sax)
trivia: Washington's strings-and-flute version of a 1934 Mexican song became her first pop top-ten hit and won the Grammy for Best Rhythm and Blues Performance. Her pianist on the album was Joe Zawinul, later of Weather Report.

track.title: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes
track.album: What a Diff'rence a Day Makes!
track.query: Dinah Washington What a Diff'rence a Day Makes What a Diff'rence a Day Makes! 1959
track.notes: Dinah Washington's 1959 Mercury single (2:31); not the 1934 Spanish original "Cuando vuelva a tu lado" nor the Dorsey Brothers version

notes: Wikipedia gives only 1959 as the recording year; a Presto listing dates the title track 19 Feb 1959, but the studio (Mercury Sound Studios vs Fine Recording Studios) differs between sources, so no exact date is used. Album-level personnel list may not apply to every track. Hit #8 on Billboard Hot 100; Grammy Hall of Fame 1998.

title: So What
original_issue: Columbia CL 1355 (LP "Kind of Blue", 17 August 1959)
personnel: Miles Davis (trumpet), Julian "Cannonball" Adderley (alto sax), John Coltrane (tenor sax), Bill Evans (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Jimmy Cobb (drums)
trivia: The opening track of Kind of Blue is built on just two modes, with a bass-and-piano call and the horns' reply. The album became the best-known modal jazz record and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1992.

track.title: So What
track.query: Miles Davis So What Kind of Blue 1959
track.notes: Columbia master take (matrix CO62291-3) from 2 Mar 1959 (9:22), as on Kind of Blue; not later live versions

notes: Date, matrix and personnel from jazzdisco (Columbia 30th Street Studio); jazzdisco credits Wynton Kelly only on "Freddie Freeloader" so Evans plays here. Wikipedia gives release as 17 Aug 1959.

title: Giant Steps
original_issue: Atlantic LP 1311 (LP "Giant Steps", February 1960)
personnel: John Coltrane (tenor sax), Tommy Flanagan (piano), Paul Chambers (bass), Art Taylor (drums)
trivia: The tune moves through key centres a major third apart at a breakneck pace, a chord pattern now known as "Coltrane changes". A first attempt in March 1959 was not used; the issued take is from May.

track.title: Giant Steps
track.query: John Coltrane Giant Steps 1959
track.notes: Atlantic matrix 3468-5 from 5 May 1959 (4:43), the album version; not the 26 Mar 1959 takes

notes: Date and matrix from jazzdisco (Atlantic Studios, New York); 26 March 1959 was an earlier, different-band attempt that Wikipedia lists with lengths 3:41 and 3:32. Wikipedia dates the album's release February 1960.

title: Goodbye Pork Pie Hat
original_issue: Columbia CL 1370 (LP "Mingus Ah Um", October 1959)

trivia: Mingus's elegy for Lester Young, who had died two months before the session; the title refers to the broad-brimmed pork pie hats Young wore. It has become one of Mingus's most-covered compositions.

track.title: Goodbye Pork Pie Hat
track.query: Charles Mingus Goodbye Pork Pie Hat Mingus Ah Um 1959
track.notes: Columbia matrix CO63342 from 12 May 1959 (5:44); not Joni Mitchell's, Jeff Beck's or later versions

notes: Date and matrix from jazzdisco; the trombonist on that session (Willie Dennis) plays on tracks 1-3 only, so none on this title. Who plays the individual solos is not confirmed. Cover artists named in the track note are examples from general knowledge.

title: Lonely Woman
original_issue: Atlantic LP 1317 (LP "The Shape of Jazz to Come", November 1959)
personnel: Ornette Coleman (alto sax), Don Cherry (trumpet), Charlie Haden (bass), Billy Higgins (drums)
trivia: The slow, keening opener of an album recorded in Los Angeles by a quartet with no piano to fix the harmony. The Shape of Jazz to Come entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2015.

track.title: Lonely Woman
track.album: The Shape of Jazz to Come
track.query: Ornette Coleman Lonely Woman The Shape of Jazz to Come 1959

title: Take Five
original_issue: Columbia 4-41479 (45 rpm single, b/w "Blue Rondo a la Turk", 21 September 1959); album "Time Out", Columbia CL 1397 (14 December 1959)
personnel: Paul Desmond (alto sax), Dave Brubeck (piano), Gene Wright (bass), Joe Morello (drums)
trivia: Drummer Joe Morello wanted a showcase for his 5/4 rhythm, so Brubeck handed Desmond the job of writing a melody over it. It was recorded at Columbia's 30th Street studio in New York and entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1996.

track.title: Take Five

track.notes: Columbia master of 1 Jul 1959 (5:24 on Time Out); not the later 7:18 live or reissue versions

artist: Horace Silver and the Jazz Messengers

trivia: The only known recording of Sonny Rollins and John Coltrane playing together: two tenor players trading choruses on a blues, backed by the rhythm section of Miles Davis's quintet. The title track was added to the Grammy Hall of Fame in 2019.

title: Brilliant Corners
original_issue: Riverside RLP 12-226 (LP "Brilliant Corners", April 1957); 45 rpm Riverside R-45-608
personnel: Ernie Henry (alto sax), Sonny Rollins (tenor sax), Thelonious Monk (piano), Oscar Pettiford (bass), Max Roach (drums)
trivia: The twisting theme and its tempo changes defeated the band: twenty-five takes were attempted without a complete one, so producer Orrin Keepnews edited the issued version from several takes. The album gave Monk his Riverside breakthrough.

track.title: Brilliant Corners

title: Fine and Mellow
original_issue: Columbia LP "The Sound of Jazz" (1958; catalogue number not verified)
personnel: Billie Holiday (vocal); Roy Eldridge and Doc Cheatham (trumpets), Vic Dickenson (trombone), Coleman Hawkins, Ben Webster and Lester Young (tenor saxes), Mal Waldron (piano), Milt Hinton (bass), Osie Johnson (drums)
trivia: A slow blues recorded for the CBS programme The Sound of Jazz, it reunited Holiday with her old friend Lester Young for the last time. Critic Nat Hentoff recalled that at rehearsals the two kept to opposite sides of the room.
